text: Unit 2, 2.1. Welcome to the latest episode of Root to Uni. Recent figures show that in a single academic year in the UK, nearly 680,000 international students came to study at universities there, accounting for 15.1% of all undergraduates and 45.4% of all post-graduates. This number has been rising and may well continue growing. So if you're hoping to study abroad, how do you do that? Here with me is Laura Collins, originally from London. Laura, you're in Canada at the moment studying at a university there. That's right. And you're studying economics and politics? Economics and political science, but yeah, close enough. Sorry. So my first question is, what can people do if they want to study overseas? Well, for people in the UK, one easy way is to apply for a degree course at a UK university that offers a year abroad. As far as I know, pretty much everything is organised by the university itself through their international connections. But you didn't do that? No, I wanted to spend the whole of my degree abroad. My advice to anyone following that route is do plenty of research as early as you can. It's not just about knowing the entrance requirements to get into a particular university, you should also consider whether it's the right place for you personally. Can you give an example of what you mean? Most colleges in the US guarantee accommodation on campus throughout your studies. That sounded good to me at first, but when I investigated college life there in more detail, there seemed to be an emphasis on the social side of university life, in clubs and so on. And that wasn't of interest? Well, I can see the appeal of that, no question. But I thought maybe I'd get too involved in social activities and I'd end up with no time for studying. In Canada, like in the UK and much of Europe, if students don't want to get too involved with anything outside academic studies, that's not really an issue. Tell us about the application process. I'd imagine that differs from country to country. Some places have centralised systems. You have one body controlling how students apply. Others are decentralised. You apply to each university individually. You need to know what the system is in the place where you're hoping to study. So in the US, you generally need to apply to each individual university. Oh, except in California, which follows a centralised system. In Canada, some areas use a centralised admission system, others don't. In the UK, everything goes through the centralised system called UCAS, the Universities and College Admissions Service, which allows students to apply to up to five degree courses at the same time. In Australia, you can do that for up to nine at once, going through the UAC, the Universities Admission Centre. Wow, I'm not sure whether I'd be confident doing that myself. Sounds complicated. It isn't really, but you have to be organised without a doubt. Get as much information as you can. Lots of students can go to an admissions advisor at their school for help, but I really believe students should be in control of their applications as much as possible. For example, for UK universities, students need a reference from a teacher in their application, and I thoroughly recommend finding a teacher you respect and who knows you well to write one for you. Also, many universities and colleges have a mission statement, a summary of their main vision. It often highlights their core values, for example, academic excellence, global citizenship or innovation in technology. I definitely advise finding out, adapting your application to show how well you might fit into their institution. Great. Another thing I'd like to ask you about.
